title: Highlight-shading relationship as a cue for the perception of translucent and transparent materials
research_question: What image features are diagnostic of the perceived translucency and transparency of 3D objects, focusing on how variations in opacity affect the non-specular component (shading pattern) but not the specular component (highlights)?

participants.description: Experiment 1: 8 naive paid volunteers (5 females, 3 males) and the author (male), average age 29.4 (SD = 5.4) years old, with normal or corrected-to-normal vision. Experiment 2: 7 subjects, all of whom participated in Experiment 1.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Computer-generated 3D objects (Bust, Lion, Buddha, Dragon) with complex shapes, rendered with two types of natural illumination (Debevec's 'Eucalyptus' and 'Building' light-probe images). For Experiment 1, objects had 9 different opacity settings (6 variable sub-surface scattering depths: 0, 0.13, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2 m; 3 variable transparencies: 25%, 50%, 100% in addition to 2m scattering). For Experiment 2, opaque objects from Exp 1 were used, and their non-specular component was decomposed into low and high spatial frequency bands, with each sub-band's contrast independently multiplied by factors (1.0, 0.6, 0.3, 0.0, -0.3, -0.6), while highlights remained intact.

measures.instrument: Five-point rating scale (0: opaque, 1-2: translucent like marble or wax, 3-4: highly translucent like jelly or glass)

findings.mechanism: Optical effects (transmission, refraction, absorption, scattering) make the image of a translucent object different from that of an opaque one.
findings.quote: It is found that the rating increases with the two optical effects.

mechanisms: The spatial and contrast relationship between specular highlights and non-specular shading patterns is a robust cue for the perceived translucency and transparency of three-dimensional objects.

Optical effects in translucent materials (transmission, refraction, absorption, scattering) primarily affect the non-specular part of the object's image, leaving specular highlights relatively constant.

As an object becomes translucent, its non-specular image component tends to have lower contrast and becomes blurred. For highly translucent or transparent objects, the non-specular component can become sharp again but with an opposite sign of contrast to an opaque object.

The visual system perceives an object as highly translucent or transparent when the non-specular image component is unpredictable or partially contrast-reversed relative to what would be expected from specular highlights.

Directional illumination on a bumpy opaque surface produces sharp shading. In translucent surfaces, scattered light makes shading patterns faint, especially for smaller structures. In highly translucent/transparent surfaces, refracted light can make the phase of spatial structure unpredictable, leading to contrast reversal in parts of the non-specular component.
The spatial congruency of patterns across different spatial frequency bands could be useful for the perception of multi-layered surfaces.
implementation_implications: Simple image manipulation of non-specular components (contrast and blur) can effectively control apparent translucency, offering an alternative to complex physical simulations in 3D computer graphics.
limitations: The experimental procedure of showing all stimuli in advance to establish a criterion might have produced a potential bias in subjects' responses.

Simple low-level image statistics (e.g., luminance contrast, skewness) cannot fully account for the perception of highly translucent surfaces, especially those involving contrast reversals in the non-specular component.

The simple translucency rating scale used in the experiment might not have captured the nuanced variations in surface appearance, such as the distinction between a multi-layered surface and a homogeneous translucent material.
